source.title: Predictable Scaling: Efficient Model Exploration via Scaling-Law Prediction
source.authors: Aishwarya Wesanekar; Sheng-Tao Yang; Jia-Wei Zang; Flavio Sales Truzzi; Chen Chen; Nader Beigiparast; Sheng-Yuan Huang; Roshanak Zilouchian Moghaddam; Vitor Cid; Colin B. Clement; Vinayak Thapliyal; S. Ament; Jihao Andreas Lin; Vincent Huang; Kai-Wen Han; Bo Jiang; Wen-Lin Chen; Chao Chen; Ashwin Kumar; Maximilian Balandat; David Eriksson; Yi-Fei Zhang; Pan Zhong

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses language-model scaling laws as context, but its experiments test prediction of relative performance gaps in recommendation models, not the claim versions about language-model pretraining losses, power laws, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The study reports recommendation-model proxy prediction results, including MAE and ranking accuracy. These concern prediction from scaled proxies, not the specified language-model power-law relationships. The paper's cited claims about LLM scaling laws are background, not its own experimental results.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates prediction of relative normalized-entropy gaps between recommendation-model hypotheses. It neither fits nor tests power-law loss curves, large-scale power-law extrapolation, compute-optimal parameter/token exponents, or downstream performance relationships. Classical scaling laws supply context rather than an experimentally tested premise. Recommendation models could bear on V5, but these experiments do not test its required power-law form.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that selected recommendation-model proxies and curve fitting enable cheaper hypothesis evaluation, reporting 79–88% compute reductions on the industrial models. They emphasize architecture-dependent fidelity and detectable failures of signal preservation, and distinguish relative-gap prediction from classical absolute-loss scaling laws. Their conclusion additionally claims perfect actionable-hypothesis ranking across both industrial models; the explicit actionable-subset result reported in Section 4 establishes this for six TS-1 hypotheses.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce the original language-model scaling-law measurements; it evaluates recommendation-model relative NE-gap prediction using scaled proxies and regression or an empirical Gaussian process.
record.method_sensitivity: Prediction quality varies by model architecture, scaling configuration, and prediction head. The paper reports especially poor rank preservation for some embedding-only or composed configurations and different performance for CTR and CVR heads.

fits_no_version.finding: Recommendation-model proxy gaps can predict full-scale hypothesis gaps, with fidelity depending on architecture, scaling configuration and predictor. TS-1 GP MAE is 0.738 times the noise floor; FM-1 CTR-1 improves from 2.150 to 0.701. Public DeepFM hash-only GP ranking reaches 0.939, whereas hash-plus-embedding ranking is −0.491.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reduced-scale recommendation-model evaluations can predict relative full-scale hypothesis performance when the selected scaling configuration preserves the relevant signal; empirical curve fitting can improve prediction accuracy.

record.problems: Experiments concern recommendation models and normalized entropy rather than language models and held-out pretraining cross-entropy. The study does not report power-law fits or exponents for the claim versions. The public evaluation uses a pool of 27 hypotheses with 10 held out; some configurations show poor or negative rank correlations. The paper notes that the public benchmark is smaller than the industrial training datasets.
record.rows_left_out: The 51 included rows cover the TS-1 and FM-1 main predictor comparisons and the public-benchmark raw-proxy and GP comparisons. Public-benchmark Linear predictor rows from Tables 10–13 were left out to remain within the 60-row limit and because they are additional predictor comparisons rather than direct evidence on the claim versions.

untested.parts: Power-law held-out language-model pretraining loss across parameters, tokens or compute over several orders of magnitude.
Power laws fitted to small runs predicting losses of runs orders of magnitude larger; relative-gap proxy prediction does not establish this.
Stable compute-optimal parameter and token growth exponents; selecting a proxy under a budget does not measure this allocation.
Loss sensitivity to architecture at fixed parameter count; the architecture interventions do not control parameter count.
Power-law form in recommendation or other non-text training regimes; smooth relative-gap transfer is a different property.
Downstream performance as a predictable function of scale or pretraining loss; hypothesis-gap prediction is a different relationship.
Dependence of power-law exponents, compute-optimal splits or curve bending on setup and fitting choices; proxy-prediction sensitivity does not measure these.

record.verdict_notes: All rows retain their existing version links and states. These are evaluations of the study's proxy method and its comparators, rather than scaling-law evidence. Negative proxy rank correlations do not challenge any listed version. Section E's ES/WAS comparison also supplies no fixed-parameter architecture test or power-law fit. No omitted result bearing on a listed version was identified.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out pretraining cross-entropy sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No prediction of language-model losses on runs orders of magnitude larger than the fitting runs.
No fixed-compute optimization of language-model parameter and token counts, or fitted growth exponents.
No controlled comparison of language-model architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Recommendation models are evaluated, but the study does not test whether power-law forms hold in another modality or training regime.
No downstream-task performance relationship with language-model scale or pretraining loss is tested.

The study reports architecture- and scaling-configuration-dependent proxy prediction quality, but does not test dependence of the specified language-model exponents or compute-optimal split on fitting choices.
